title: Dashboard Mount jog pad fires a 500 ms pulse guide instead of a slew - the arrows do nothing a user can see
summary: The pad's onDirection called mountCommandService.pulseGuide(direction) with the service's default 500 ms — about four arcseconds at guide rate, invisible on the card's own RA/Dec readout — and because it was an InkWell onTap, a 2 s press-and-hold produced exactly one pulse. Replaced it with a real hold-to-jog pad. New MountJogControls (a ConsumerStatefulWidget in mount_control_card.dart) plus a pure-logic module mount_jog.dart: pointer-down starts, pointer-up/cancel stops. When the driver advertises canMoveAxis the pad drives DeviceBackend.mountMoveAxis (axis 0 = RA/Az, axis 1 = Dec/Alt, sign = N/E positive, matching the backend contract and the native INDI mapping) and a new 'Jog' speed selector sits under it offering 1x/8x/64x/400x sidereal, dropping any rate above a driver-reported maxSlewRate and appending that ceiling as 'Max'; default is the 8x centring speed. Mounts with no MoveAxis but with pulse guiding fall back to REPEATED 500 ms pulses while held, and the row under the pad says so in words instead of looking like a slew pad. Mounts that can do neither disable the pad and say why (unknown capabilities fail closed). Safety, which the original had no need for and the new one does: the axis stop is sent on release, on pointer-cancel, on widget dispose (the backend that received the start is captured in a field because Riverpod's ref is already dead inside dispose), and by a 30 s hold watchdog — a MoveAxis with no matching stop drives the mount into the pier. The arrows also carry a Semantics label plus a tap action that performs a bounded start/stop nudge, since assistive tech cannot express press-and-hold.
test: packages/skotiq_app/test/screens/dashboard/mount_jog_pad_test.dart — 11 tests driving the REAL MountControlCard with pointer gestures against a recording DeviceBackend and a recording MountCommandService. Key ones: 'holding an arrow slews the axis and releasing stops it' (asserts zero pulseGuide calls, one mountMoveAxis with a positive rate on axis 0, still exactly one call two seconds in, then a rate-0 stop on release); 'the jog speed selector is what sets the slew rate' (picks 64x from the dropdown, asserts the sent rate is 64 x sidereal); 'north and south drive the secondary axis with opposite signs'; 'a held jog is stopped by the watchdog rather than running on'; 'tearing the card down mid-press still stops the axis'; 'a mount with no MoveAxis repeats guide pulses and says so' (>1 pulse while held, none after release, no MoveAxis, and the 'Guide pulses' label present); 'a mount that can do neither disables the pad and explains'; 'a screen-reader tap jogs and then stops on its own'.
revert_check: Replaced the pad's Listener (onPointerDown/_startJog, onPointerUp/_stopJog, onPointerCancel/_stopJog) with the shipped wiring — a GestureDetector whose onTap calls `ref.read(mountCommandServiceProvider).pulseGuide(direction)` — in mount_control_card.dart:~525. 6 of the 11 tests FAILED (every gesture-driven one); restored and all 11 pass. Full owned-area suites: 276 pass.
needs_shared_change: native/skotiq_native/bridge/src/device_capabilities.rs:~3103 — the SIMULATOR mount advertises can_move_axis: false (the struct default) and no max_slew_rate, even though device_manager/ops/mount.rs:~2450 DOES implement mount_move_axis for DriverType::Simulator. So on the sim rig the new pad resolves to the pulse fallback and the real slew path stays unexercised. Set can_move_axis: true, axis_count: 2 and a representative max_slew_rate (e.g. Some(4.0)) there. Second, related: that same simulator branch of mount_move_axis only flips status.slewing and never integrates RA/Dec, so even with the capability the coordinates would not move while jogging — worth making the sim advance the pointing at the commanded rate, otherwise the simulator still fails in the pass-making direction for this control.
caveats: Verified by test, not on hardware. The axis/sign convention follows the documented DeviceBackend.mountMoveAxis contract ('positive = N/E') and the native INDI mapping; an ASCOM mount whose primary axis is inverted would jog mirrored, which only real hardware can confirm. The rate ladder is offered in full when a driver reports no maxSlewRate — a driver that rejects a rate surfaces its own error via the snackbar rather than being silently clamped to something we invented.

title: Flat wizard's "Flat capture failed - no frames were saved" gives no reason and no next step
summary: The verifier's sharper diagnosis was right: the reason IS computed and then dropped. flat_wizard_service.dart returns errorMessage 'Max exposure reached but still under target' (and siblings), flat_wizard_provider.dart stores it via setWarningMessage, but NO widget under screens/flat_wizard/ ever read state.warningMessage — the only thing rendered was state.errorMessage, which _setFinalStatus overwrites with the generic literal. Two changes. (1) The action-buttons banner now renders state.warningMessage in its own amber banner (with a dismiss that calls the already-existing notifier.clearWarning), so the solver's per-filter reason reaches the screen at all — including on partial runs, which previously showed nothing. (2) A new flat_failure_diagnosis.dart turns the wizard's terminal state into numbers under the red banner: it reads aduHistory plus the global min/max exposure and target percentage and names the failure — panel-not-illuminating first ('R: brightness barely changed while the exposure grew 176x (0.17 s to 30.0 s, 1364 ADU against 1049)' + 'The sensor is not being illuminated. Check the flat panel is switched on...'), then the exposure ceiling ('at the 30.0 s maximum exposure the frame only reached 20120 ADU, short of the 50% target'), then the exposure floor (too bright), then non-convergence — each with the thing to change. It deliberately does NOT restate an absolute target ADU: that conversion needs the camera's bit depth, which the wizard state does not carry, so the target is quoted as the histogram percentage the operator typed. With no measurements at all it returns null and only the wizard's own message shows.
test: packages/skotiq_app/test/screens/flat_wizard/flat_failure_banner_test.dart — four widget tests pumping the real FlatWizardScreen with the notifier pinned to a terminal state, asserting on RENDERED text. 'names an unilluminated panel instead of just "failed"' replays the audited ramp verbatim (0.17 s/1049 ADU -> 30 s/1364 ADU) and asserts the 176x wording, the ADU pair, the panel next-step AND the solver's own 'R: Max exposure reached but still under target'. The others cover the ceiling case, the floor case, and the no-measurements case (which must show only the wizard message and no invented diagnosis).
revert_check: Two separate reverts. (a) Replaced `final diagnosis = state.errorMessage != null ? diagnoseFlatFailure(state) : null;` with `const FlatFailureDiagnosis? diagnosis = null;` in action_buttons.dart:17 — 3 of 4 tests failed (0 widgets with the diagnosis text). (b) Restored and instead disabled the warning banner block (`if (state.warningMessage != null)` -> `if (false)`) at action_buttons.dart:81 — the first test failed on the missing 'R: Max exposure reached but still under target'. Restored both; all 4 pass.
caveats: The two thresholds that classify 'ADU did not respond' (exposure grew >= 4x while ADU grew < 1.5x) are heuristics, named constants with the reasoning in comments. A genuinely non-linear panel could in principle be misdescribed; the banner still quotes the raw measurements next to the claim so the operator can see what it was reasoning from.

title: Collaborative Sky still says "No collaborative mosaics on this hub yet" right after you publish one
summary: collaborativeMosaicsProvider (and the detail/attribution families) are plain non-autoDispose FutureProviders, so the empty answer the Collaborate surface got when it opened was cached for the life of the container. The only invalidate() in the repo was inside the screen header's manual refresh icon. mosaic_project_controller.publishToHub() called `await load()`, which reloads only that controller's own project row, so nothing told the shared listing it was stale. Added a `_reloadAfterHubMutation()` on MosaicProjectController that reloads AND fires a new `onHubStateChanged` hook, and routed EVERY hub-mutating action through it (publish, claim, release, force-release, upload, assemble, join) while leaving local-only integrate/stitch on the bare load() so they do not trigger needless hub round-trips. mosaicProjectControllerProvider wires the hook to a new shared `invalidateCollaborativeMosaicState(ref)` helper that owns the full provider set in one place; the screen header's _refresh and the Collaborative Sky detail screen's _join now call the same helper, so the set cannot drift.
test: packages/skotiq_app/test/screens/collaborative_sky/collab_mosaic_publish_refresh_test.dart — drives the REAL mosaicProjectControllerProvider in a ProviderContainer against an in-memory DB and a fake hub whose listMosaics() answers from a catalogue publishProject() appends to. It warms collaborativeMosaicsProvider with the empty answer FIRST (the field ordering), then publishes and asserts the next read returns ['M31 Wide Field'] and that listMosaics was hit a second time. A second test does the same for claimPanel.
revert_check: Deleted the single production wiring line `onHubStateChanged: () => invalidateCollaborativeMosaicState(ref),` from the mosaicProjectControllerProvider body. Both tests FAILED: publish got `Actual: MappedListIterable<CollabMosaic, String>:[]` against `Expected: ['M31 Wide Field']`, claim got listCalls 1 vs 2. Restored; collaborative_sky (51) and mosaic (47) suites both fully green.
caveats: refreshStatus() and downloadOutput() intentionally still use the plain load(): they read hub state rather than change it. Could not be driven end-to-end against a live hub — no skotiq_hub runs on this machine — so this is verified by the provider-level test, exactly where the defect lives.

title: The Smart Night dashboard prompt never appears even with its toggle on and every documented precondition met
summary: Root cause was a frozen clock, exactly as the verifier diagnosed. smart_night_prompt_card.dart declared `smartNightPromptNowProvider = Provider<DateTime>((ref) => DateTime.now())` — a non-autoDispose Provider, so the single DateTime.now() captured on first read was cached for the life of the container. `_equipmentReadyGraceElapsed` did `_equipmentReadySince ??= now` then `now.difference(_equipmentReadySince!)`, which was therefore permanently Duration.zero: the 60 s equipment-ready grace could never elapse, canPlan was permanently false, and the card returned SizedBox.shrink() forever. Replaced the cached DateTime with a clock FUNCTION (`smartNightPromptClockProvider = Provider<DateTime Function()>((ref) => DateTime.now)`) that the card calls on every rebuild. Also fixed the second half of the trap: the 60 s wake-up Timer was armed with `_graceTimer ??= Timer(...)` and left non-null after firing, so it could never re-arm; the callback now clears the handle first.
test: packages/skotiq_app/test/screens/dashboard/smart_night_prompt_card_test.dart — two new tests. 'shows the prompt once the equipment-ready grace has elapsed' injects a moving clock and asserts the rendered card ('Hardware ready - build tonight's plan?' + 'Plan Tonight') and smartNightAutoPromptShowingProvider == true. 'the production clock advances the grace window' deliberately does NOT override the clock provider — it shortens the grace to 200 ms, sleeps 300 ms of REAL time via tester.runAsync, and asserts the card renders; that one is the guard on the shipped provider definition.
revert_check: Reverted the provider body to caching semantics (`Provider<DateTime Function()>((ref) { final frozen = DateTime.now(); return () => frozen; })`). 'the production clock advances the grace window' FAILED at test line 317 (findsOneWidget -> zero widgets). Restored; all 8 tests in the file pass.
caveats: The verifier also flagged `if (draftAsync.isLoading || draftAsync.valueOrNull != null) return SizedBox.shrink()` as a possible second suppressor. Left alone deliberately: the pending-draft lookup is a DB read that does resolve, and suppressing the prompt while the answer is unknown is correct. Adding a speculative timeout there would have been relocating, not fixing.
